questions.question: What makes an object "iterable" in JavaScript?
options: Implementing a method keyed by Symbol.iterator that returns an iterator object with a .next() method
Being created with the Array constructor
Any plain object is automatically iterable
questions.explanation: The iterable protocol requires a Symbol.iterator method returning an object whose .next() yields { value, done } pairs — plain objects don't implement this by default.

questions.question: Why does `for (const x of plainObject)` throw an error while `for (const x of someArray)` works fine?
options: Arrays implement Symbol.iterator built in; plain objects don't implement the iterable protocol unless you add it yourself
This is a bug that will eventually be fixed
Objects can never be looped over in JavaScript
questions.explanation: for...of requires the iterable protocol; built-ins like arrays, strings, Maps, and Sets implement it, but plain object literals do not unless explicitly given a Symbol.iterator method.

questions.question: What does calling a generator function (`function*`) do, compared to a regular function?
options: It immediately runs the entire function body, just like a regular function
It returns an iterator without running the body yet; execution happens incrementally, pausing at each `yield`
It throws an error unless awaited
It behaves identically to a regular function in every way
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function returns an iterator object; the function body only executes up to the next yield each time .next() is called.

questions.question: Why can a generator represent an infinite sequence (like all natural numbers) without crashing or hanging?
options: Because it pre-computes a very large but finite array in memory
Because it only computes the next value lazily when the consumer asks for it, rather than producing all values upfront
Because infinite loops are optimized away by the engine
It actually cannot — this always crashes
questions.explanation: Generators are lazy — each yield pauses until the next value is explicitly requested, so a consumer can take as many or as few values as it wants without the generator ever needing to finish.
